title: Agent loop & stop conditions
kicker: Know what finished, paused, or failed
summary: Follow custom tools through the compiled graph, distinguish messages from pending calls, and inspect every stopping-policy class with reproducible runtime evidence.

sections.title: The short answer: no new tool calls is the normal exit, not the whole contract
sections.body:
In the ordinary tool loop, a new assistant message with an empty tool_calls list leaves the model/tools cycle. Applicable completion hooks still run before graph END. Structured-output requirements, middleware routing, and direct-return tools can change that path.

The runtime checks structured message fields and configured routes—not whether the text says “Done.” Finishing one tool call is also different from finishing the agent invocation: the model normally receives the result and decides what to do next.

Use the right unit of completion

UnitWhat finished?What can still happen?
Model responseOne model request returned an assistant message.Tools, another model request, validation, or completion hooks.
Tool callOne call produced a result or error.Other calls from the same response and the next model decision.
Agent invocationThe graph reached its terminal path without a pending interrupt.A future invocation on the same saved thread.
Subagent invocationThat child graph finished.The parent reads its report and continues its own loop.
Application taskYour acceptance criteria were met.This needs application checks; graph END alone does not establish it.

Verification scope: this chapter pairs source inspection with real compiled-agent probes using deterministic model fixtures. The tools, graph routing, checkpoints, interrupts, and exceptions execute; the fixture responses are not genuine LLM reasoning or provider integration evidence.

sections.title: Adding tools changes available handlers, not a fixed tool pipeline
sections.body:
Passing tools=[search, calculate] makes those capabilities available alongside middleware-provided tools. It does not mean “search, then calculate,” and it does not create one ordinary LangGraph node per tool. A ToolNode dispatches the requested handler by name.

Inspect the actual compiled configuration

The verification run extracts graph nodes and edges from create_deep_agent with a controlled model and custom tools. The default graph includes model, tools, PatchToolCallsMiddleware.before_agent, and _ParentNotifierMiddleware.after_agent, plus start/end sentinels. The evidence contains the actual serialized topology, not a reconstruction from class names.

  1. Construction registers tools and middleware. Built-in file tools and the optional inline-task tool share the dispatcher with caller tools. Capability filtering can change what the model sees without removing every registered handler.
  2. Invocation enters startup hooks, then the model path. Wrapper middleware can shape model/tool calls without appearing as a separate graph node. A graph image is therefore not a complete list of policies executed inside a node.
  3. Conditional routing chooses the next destination. Pending ordinary calls dispatch to tools; the normal no-call path proceeds through completion hooks. Completed tool work ordinarily returns to the model.
  4. Configuration can change the topology. Human review, additional before/after hooks, profiles, and structured-output choices may add nodes or destinations. Inspect your own graph rather than copying the probe topology as a universal diagram.

Illustrative inspection with your configured model and credentials:

from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from langchain.tools import tool


@tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two integers."""
    return a + b


agent = create_deep_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    tools=[add],
)
print(agent.get_graph().draw_mermaid())

This code inspects the graph; it does not invoke a user task. The website does not execute it. The credential-free verification script uses a controlled model instead. Read the measured topology and case results for the tested configuration.

sections.title: A tool request, its result, and a final answer are different messages
sections.body:
A tool call never needs to “turn into” ordinary text. The original assistant message remains a record of the requested work. A separate tool result answers its call ID; a later assistant message can request more work or finish.

Illustrative message objects, not a captured run:

from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, ToolMessage

request = AIMessage(
    content="I will calculate that.",
    tool_calls=[{
        "name": "add",
        "args": {"a": 2, "b": 2},
        "id": "call_1",
        "type": "tool_call",
    }],
)
result = ToolMessage(content="4", tool_call_id="call_1")
answer = AIMessage(content="2 + 2 = 4.", tool_calls=[])

messages = [request, result, answer]
  1. Inspect the latest relevant assistant message. Old tool requests can remain in history after their results are recorded. A history-wide search for any tool_calls would incorrectly keep completed work alive.
  2. Correlate results by ID. The result's tool_call_id identifies the request it answers. Message order and visible text are not substitutes for that identity.
  3. Distinguish answered calls from an exit. “No outstanding calls from the last request” normally means the model can interpret the results. “The new assistant response requests no tools” is the ordinary exit signal.

Text is not control flow: “Done” plus a real tool call still requests execution. An empty answer, a clarification question, or a truncated-looking answer without tool calls can leave the ordinary loop. None establishes task correctness.

sections.title: Read the router as ordered guards, not a single if statement
sections.body:
Deep Agents owns harness assembly; LangChain owns the model/tools routing. This verification uses LangChain 1.4.8. Its version-pinned router source matches the installed file byte-for-byte; a local source snapshot and hashes are retained. The normal model-to-tools decision has the following precedence.

  1. Honor an explicit middleware jump first. A supported jump_to can route to the model, tools, or the configured end destination before the ordinary tool-call checks.
  2. Handle missing assistant history. If no assistant message remains, this router takes its end destination. This is a defensive branch, not a recommended way to signal successful work.
  3. Check the latest assistant's call list. An empty list takes the normal end destination. Completion hooks may still run; “end destination” is not necessarily the bare END sentinel.
  4. Dispatch pending ordinary calls. Exclude calls already answered by correlated tool messages and calls reserved for structured output. Remaining real calls are sent to the tool dispatcher.
  5. Recognize a fresh structured response. If no real calls remain and this invocation produced validated structured output, take the end destination.
  6. Continue when calls were already answered synthetically. Calls can remain on an assistant message even though middleware supplied their results. With no fresh structured response, route back to the model—not automatically to END.

The tools-to-model decision is separate: eligible direct-return batches and schema receipts whose status is not error can end; ordinary completed tool work returns to the model. Receipt status is not proof of schema validity: see the mixed-batch pitfall below.

A graph configured for structured output without ordinary tools uses another continuation check, so the no-call shorthand must not be applied to every configuration.

Why this chapter records dependency versions separately

The upstream Deep Agents pin declares a compatible LangChain range, not one immutable dependency graph. The website's source atlas contains Deep Agents implementation and tests; it does not silently pretend dependency internals belong to that snapshot. Reproducing this verification requires its recorded requirements, and other installed versions must be checked independently.

sections.title: Normal continuation and completion scenarios
sections.body:
These cases explain the default loop before advanced policies change it. “Ends” means an invocation reaches its terminal path; it does not certify the answer or delete the thread.

ScenarioNormal next actionInterpretation
First response has no tool callsCompletion hooks, then END unless redirectedThe model can answer without using an available tool.
Response says “Done” but contains a tool callExecute the pending callVisible completion wording does not cancel structured work.
One ordinary tool returnsAsk the model againA ToolMessage is an input to the next decision, not normally the final answer.
Several calls share one assistant responseProcess their results, then continue the model pathTools need not be separate named graph nodes; parallel execution does not mean a fixed tool sequence.
Later model response requests another toolRepeat the cycleThere is no rule requiring a single tool round.
Later model response has no tool callsCompletion hooks, then the terminal pathOriginal call-bearing messages remain in history.
No-call response is empty, incomplete, or asks the user a questionThe ordinary no-call route can still endCompletion is control flow, not usefulness or factual correctness.
Provider finish metadata says “length,” but the normalized message has no callsThe ordinary router does not use that string as its completion testInspect truncation separately; a token-limit response is not a reliable accepted answer.
The response has only invalid_tool_calls, with an empty valid tool_calls listThe measured ordinary route ends that invocation without automatically retrying the malformed callOn a later invocation, startup repair can add the missing error receipt. Parsing failure and ordinary argument-validation feedback are different paths.

In a plain LangChain agent, no registered ordinary tools can remove the ordinary tool loop entirely. In Deep Agents, tools=[] only removes caller additions: middleware can still provide file and task tools. Do not assume an empty caller list creates a model-only Deep Agents graph.

The receipt-order probes use max_concurrency=1 for reproducibility. Their observed ordering is not a promise that arbitrary multi-tool batches execute serially in production.

sections.title: Direct-return tools and tool-issued control flow
sections.body:
return_direct=True is tool configuration, not a magic string in its returned content. In the tested dependency, direct-return termination requires a nonempty set of relevant executed client-side tools and all of them to be direct-return.

Tool batchRouting consequenceConsumer caution
One executed direct-return toolCan take the end destination without another model turnThe final result can be a tool message, not newly authored assistant prose.
Several executed tools, all direct-returnThe all-direct condition is satisfiedCollect the actual results; do not expect a model-generated synthesis.
Direct-return mixed with an ordinary toolThe all-direct shortcut does not applyThe model normally gets the batch results and continues.
A tool returns text containing “END” or “Done”No special graph route follows from that textData is not a Command.
An ordinary tool returns Command(goto=END)The measured factory graph still follows its tools-to-model conditional edgeA Command destination does not suppress the other scheduled graph routing; this is not a universal stop switch.
A terminal Command is combined with an applicable direct-return policyThe normal tools-to-model continuation can be avoided under that configured pathVerify the actual configuration and final state rather than generalizing from a single destination field.

The dependency resolves executed tool identities from correlated results when applicable, including redirected review calls. Do not generalize a direct-return decision from the name originally proposed by the model alone. Provider-hosted tools operate inside a provider request and are a separate boundary from the local dispatcher.

Measured correction: “a tool returns a Command targeting END” is insufficient evidence that this assembled agent stops. The runtime probe checks whether another model call occurs. Commands and the graph's configured edges must be considered together.

When direct return is appropriate

Use it when the tool result itself is the intended consumer output and skipping another model interpretation is deliberate. It is not a guarantee that the result is safe, correctly formatted for your UI, or sufficient to satisfy the user's larger task.

sections.title: Structured output adds its own success and recovery paths
sections.body:
response_format asks the agent to produce a validated result, not merely an assistant sentence. Deep Agents forwards this configuration to LangChain. Native provider output and tool-based structured output use different machinery.

ScenarioMeasured or configured next actionWhat to inspect
Valid provider-native structured responseParse and store the result, then finish the configured pathThe current invocation's structured_response, not a stale previous turn. The probe verifies local parsing, not provider-side constrained generation.
Invalid provider-native responseThe measured local validation raises after one model call; there is no implicit ToolStrategy-style retryStructuredOutputValidationError and pending graph state.
Valid tool-strategy structured responseHandle the output-schema call and finishThis call represents output construction, not ordinary external work.
A valid schema call and a real tool call occur togetherThe pending real work still executes before terminationValidated output does not silently erase other requested work.
Schema-only ToolStrategy validation or multiple-output error, with recovery enabledReturn corrective feedback and ask the model againThe measured schema-only fixtures take another model turn before accepting a valid response.
A schema error and a real tool call occur together, with recovery enabledThe real tool executes, then the measured invocation ends without a retryBoth invalid-schema and multiple-output probes stop after one model call with structured_response=None. This is a version-specific completion pitfall, not successful validation.
ToolStrategy validation with handle_errors=FalseRaise without a recovery turnThe propagated validation error; no manufactured valid response.
Plain text without a schema call, in a graph with ordinary toolsThe measured Deep Agents invocation ends after one model callstructured_response=None: requesting a schema does not override this router's no-call exit.
Plain text without a schema call, with ToolStrategy and no ordinary toolsThe measured dependency-only graph calls the model again, then accepts a valid schema responseDeep Agents ships built-in ordinary tools: passing tools=[] does not select this no-ordinary-tools dependency topology.

Why the mixed-error batch can end prematurely

  1. Corrective text is not an error status. The pinned factory creates feedback ToolMessages without setting status="error"; the observed status is success.
  2. The pending real tool still runs. Its ordinary result reaches the separate tools-to-model router alongside the corrective schema receipt.
  3. The router sees a completion signal. A schema receipt whose status is not error triggers the end destination—even though no validated result was produced.

Both cases were reproduced through create_deep_agent. Compare schema-feedback creation with the tools-router exit guard; do not generalize the schema-only recovery result to mixed batches.

Schema validity is not business validity: a correctly typed object can still contain an incorrect claim. Keep schema completion, model-loop completion, and application acceptance as separate checks.

sections.title: Middleware can prevent, redirect, or reopen a natural stop
sections.body:
The normal no-call branch is not the final authority when configured middleware can change destinations. Before/after hooks and model/tool wrappers have different responsibilities; only supported routing fields and hooks affect graph transitions.

  1. End before ordinary dispatch. An explicit supported jump_to="end" can take precedence over the model's proposed calls. Treat this as a policy-controlled exit, not evidence those calls executed.
  2. Request another model decision. A supported jump_to="model" can continue even after a no-call response. Route-to-tools likewise needs a valid tool-call state; a destination alone does not supply missing arguments.
  3. Run completion hooks. A no-call result can enter after_agent rather than END directly. An after-agent hook can send the graph back to the model. Inspect the final destination, not just the last model response.
  4. Keep wrappers separate from node hooks. A wrapper can transform requests, results, or state without becoming a graph node. Unsupported Command routing from a wrapper is not equivalent to an allowed before/after-hook jump.

Opt-in call budgets have explicit exit policies

The probes also install LangChain call-limit middleware. These are deliberate additions, not automatic guarantees from Deep Agents' large recursion limit.

Configured policyMeasured boundaryOutcome
ModelCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=1, exit_behavior="end")One model call and its requested tool complete; the next model request is blockedTerminal limit message rather than another model turn.
Same model limit with exit_behavior="error"The next model request reaches the limiterModelCallLimitExceededError, not successful completion.
ToolCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=0, exit_behavior="continue")The requested tool is not executedCorrelated error feedback, then another model decision.
Same zero tool budget with exit_behavior="end"The requested tool is not executedTerminal error receipt without another model turn.
Same zero tool budget with exit_behavior="error"The requested tool is not executedToolCallLimitExceededError.

Shipped example: rubric grading

Optional RubricMiddleware grades a natural stop. A needs_revision result injects feedback and jumps to the model. Its other terminal statuses include satisfied, failed, max_iterations_reached, and grader_error. The default cap is three grader iterations; reaching it does not mean the rubric passed.

All five rubric paths are exercised with a controlled grader. In this runtime, private _rubric_* fields appear in agent.get_state(config).values but are filtered from the ordinary invoke result. Inspect the saved rubric status rather than assuming the last draft or a missing output key means grading passed.

Model profiles can also install final-answer guards or retries. Read the shipped profile effects before assuming two models produce identical graph control flow. A provider error is not automatically retried just because the SDK supports middleware.

sections.title: A human-review interrupt is a pause, not END
sections.body:
An interrupted graph can return control to its caller without completing its terminal path. Persisting the same thread with a checkpointer makes a later resume possible. The fact that invoke returned, or a stream stopped yielding, does not by itself distinguish completed from paused.

Resume decisions change what happens to the pending call

DecisionEffect on reviewed workDoes the decision itself finish the agent?
approveAllow the proposed call to continue through normal execution checks.No. Its result normally returns to the model.
editExecute the approved replacement name/arguments where permitted.No. Re-enter validation and policy for the actual final call.
rejectDo not execute the rejected operation; supply the review outcome.Not inherently. The model can explain or propose another permitted action.
respondProvide a result without executing the proposed tool.Not inherently. The model can process that result and continue.

Resume the exact interrupted thread with the decisions payload; another thread does not approve this pending action. Parent and child graphs can have different approval policies. A terminal-looking last assistant message does not cancel the interrupt.

Pause is not rollback: approval gates the reviewed operation. Earlier successful tool effects may already exist, and rewinding or resuming graph state does not promise to undo external writes.

sections.title: Failure, retry, cancellation, and limits are not successful completion
sections.body:
Separate an error returned as model-visible data from an exception escaping the graph. A tool message with error status can still be followed by recovery; an unhandled exception is not a final answer. Retry policies must be configured at the boundary that owns the failure.

ScenarioExecution outcomeOperational consequence
Tool validation or execution error converted to a ToolMessageThe model can receive feedback and continue.Inspect tool status and the later result; do not interpret an error message as graph END.
Unhandled tool exceptionThe invocation fails.A successful earlier side effect is not automatically undone.
Unhandled model/provider exceptionThe invocation fails unless an installed policy handles it.Do not assume unlimited automatic retries.
Recursion/step limit exhaustedLangGraph raises GraphRecursionError.This is a protective failure, not a model decision that the task is finished.
Explicit async deadline expiresThe caller's timeout mechanism stops awaiting and requests cancellation.Model/provider/remote-tool work may need its own cancellation contract.
Caller explicitly cancels the async taskLocal execution observes cancellation where supported.Cleanup must run; already-started external effects need separate handling.
Context remains too large after bounded recoveryContextOverflowError propagates.Reduce irreducible prompts, tool schemas, recent payloads, or configured output allocation.
A client disconnects from a remote streamThe client stops observing; server behavior is transport/application-specific.Do not equate loss of UI output with confirmed server cancellation.

Deep Agents configures recursion_limit=9_999 by default. This counts graph execution steps under LangGraph semantics, not 9,999 guaranteed tool calls, a wall-clock deadline, or a spending limit. Override invocation configuration deliberately and enforce independent time, cost, and acceptance limits in the application.

Illustrative application-owned async deadline:

import asyncio


async def invoke_with_deadline(agent, inputs):
    async with asyncio.timeout(30):
        return await agent.ainvoke(inputs)

The verification probes use short controlled waits rather than a real slow provider. A timed-out request is reported as timed out, never as a successful model answer.

sections.title: A child ending, a parent ending, and background work ending are different
sections.body:
Stopping conditions belong to an execution scope. A child report is a result for its caller; the parent's loop and external background runs have their own lifecycles.

  1. Inline child completion returns to the parent. The task tool awaits the child, extracts its report, and returns a correlated tool message plus eligible state updates. The parent can then call another tool or answer. Child END is not parent END.
  2. Remote launch returns before remote completion. A background start tool records thread/run identities after creation. The parent can finish its own invocation while that remote work remains running or waiting.
  3. A fresh notification can reopen a natural stop. Async background reconciliation also runs after an apparent final answer. Newly observed notifications can request another model turn; the mere existence of running tasks does not force a blind loop.
  4. Waiting is not a completed remote report. The SDK examines both run and thread state to distinguish success, interrupted human review, replacement/cancellation, and newer work.

The local graph probes cover inline child-to-parent continuation. Real hosted background execution, notification delivery, and disconnect behavior are source-inspected boundaries unless explicitly recorded as executed in the evidence. No remote service or credential-backed provider was contacted by the loop verification.

Application acceptance is another boundary: even a terminal rubric status can be failed, max_iterations_reached, or grader_error. Likewise, parent END does not establish every background job finished. Read structured statuses instead of treating the last visible sentence as a universal success signal.

sections.title: Verify completion from state and evidence, not just final text
sections.body:
52 executable probe cases passed. They run real compiled graphs with controlled provider responses, real Python tool handlers, checkpoints, schema parsing, human-review resume, call budgets, and cancellation. They are a focused verification harness—not the upstream test suite or a live-model evaluation.

Recorded runtime

ComponentVerified version
Conda CPython3.12.12
Deep Agents0.7.32 at the unchanged website source pin
LangChain / core1.4.8 / 1.7.6
LangGraph / prebuilt1.2.20 / 1.1.1

Each case in the evidence JSON records its graph owner, model calls and inputs, correlated results, side-effect receipts, checkpoint destinations, and any relevant exception or rubric state. Some probes isolate the dependency with create_agent; the others execute create_deep_agent. That ownership is explicit rather than treating a dependency-only check as a full-harness test.

Inspect state and the actual call outcome

For a checkpointed graph, a response object or a closed stream can represent a pause. Pair the execution outcome with its snapshot; a complete-looking sentence can precede additional hook-driven work.

Illustrative inspection after invoking a graph configured with a checkpointer:

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "review-example"}}
snapshot = agent.get_state(config)

print(snapshot.next)        # Scheduled graph destinations, if any.
print(snapshot.interrupts)  # Pending interrupt information.
print(snapshot.values)      # State, not proof of task correctness.
  1. Identify the executing scope. Is this one provider response, a tool, an inline child, the parent invocation, or a hosted background run?
  2. Check control-flow evidence. Inspect pending graph work and interrupts; preserve propagated errors, cancellations, and timeout outcomes instead of converting them into empty success responses.
  3. Inspect the latest normalized assistant message. Correlate tool results by ID, then account for structured output, direct-return configuration, explicit commands, and before/after hooks.
  4. Check application acceptance separately. Validate the artifact, records processed, tests, rubric result, or other concrete success condition required by the task.

Reproduce the credential-free probes

The public repository includes the Python verification script, pinned requirements, and the inspected dependency source snapshot. Create a project-local virtual environment using your Conda interpreter, install the requirements, then run .venv/bin/python verify_agent_loop.py from the repository root. Verification dependencies are not required to serve this static website.

Source-only external boundaries and what “all scenarios” means

The chapter covers the inspected factory's routing classes, Deep Agents completion policies, checkpointed human review, and caller-owned stopping/failure boundaries. Actual hosted-provider enforcement, provider-hosted server tools, real remote background reconciliation, and transport disconnect handling were not exercised. Their ownership and limits are source-inspected. Arbitrary third-party tools, middleware, or remote services can add behavior; this is not a claim of universal exhaustive testing.
